Gregory the Theologian

Icons

Saints

St. Gregory the Theologian

St. Gregory of Nazianzus

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

St. Gregory the Theologian is the Cappadocian bishop and teacher associated with Constantinople and the confession of the Trinity. He is not St. Gregory of Nyssa, St. Gregory Palamas, or St. Gregory the Dialogist.

[1] January 25, Reading, identity and Cappadocian background

What is depicted

The illustrated Russian icon is catalogued as sixteenth century and explicitly identifies St. Gregory of Nazianzus. His episcopal vestments, raised hand, and book belong to this historical depiction; their presence alone would not identify an otherwise unnamed bishop.

[2] Exact artwork file: Description, Creator, Date, Credit and licence fields; complete downloaded image visually compared

History and tradition

The Greek church reading follows Gregory’s friendship with Basil and his theological preaching in Constantinople. It connects his title Theologian with the depth of his teaching about the Trinity. The primary passage below is his own theological oration in a named public-domain translation.

[1] January 25, Reading, Constantinople and the theological orations

Published explanation

XIV. What is our quarrel and dispute with both? To us there is One God, for the Godhead is One, and all that proceedeth from Him is referred to One, though we believe in Three Persons. For one is not more and another less God; nor is One before and another after; nor are They divided in will or parted in power; nor can you find here any of the qualities of divisible things; but the Godhead is, to speak concisely, undivided in separate Persons; and there is one mingling of Light, as it were of three suns joined to each other. When then we look at the Godhead, or the First Cause, or the Monarchia, that which we conceive is One; but when we look at the Persons in Whom the Godhead dwells, and at Those Who timelessly and with equal glory have their Being from the First Cause--there are Three Whom we worship.

[3] Oration 31 (Fifth Theological Oration), section XIV
